questions.question: Trace the chain from unequal heating to wind, and explain why a low-pressure cell brings rain while a high-pressure cell brings clear skies.
questions.expected_answer: Heating makes air expand, become less dense and rise, which lifts the column away from the surface so surface pressure falls and a low-pressure cell forms; cooling makes air contract, become denser and sink, piling molecules onto the surface so pressure rises and a high forms. Wind is then simply the horizontal movement of air from the high toward the low, and its strength is read from isobar spacing — packed isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and a strong wind. The weather difference comes from the vertical motion, not the horizontal one. In a low the air rises, expands and cools adiabatically, its vapour condenses, and cloud and rain follow, so lows are unsettled and wet. In a high the air subsides, is compressed and warms adiabatically, so relative humidity falls, cloud evaporates and the weather is clear, dry and settled.

questions.question: Describe the tri-cellular circulation and explain, using the seasonal migration of the pressure belts, why the south-western Cape has winter rainfall while the interior has summer rainfall.
questions.expected_answer: Three vertical loops operate in each hemisphere. The Hadley cell runs from the equator to about 30 degrees: air rises at the equatorial low, moves poleward aloft, cools, subsides at 30 degrees to form the subtropical highs and returns at the surface as the trade winds; it is the strongest because heating drives it directly. The Ferrel cell between about 30 and 60 degrees is indirect, driven by its neighbours, with the westerlies as its surface wind. The polar cell has cold dense air sinking at the pole, flowing equatorward as the polar easterlies and rising again at the polar front near 60 degrees, where the jet streams run high overhead. The belts migrate about five degrees with the overhead sun. In winter they shift north, bringing the westerlies and their cold fronts over the south-western Cape and giving Cape Town winter rain, while the continental high dominates the interior with clear, cold, dry conditions. In summer they shift south, the westerlies retreat over the ocean and moist tropical air reaches Limpopo and Gauteng, giving the interior its summer rainfall.

questions.question: Explain how a berg wind forms, calculate the temperature of air that leaves the plateau edge at 1 800 m and 12 degrees Celsius and descends to sea level, and account for the fire danger it creates.
questions.expected_answer: A berg wind occurs when air is drawn from the interior plateau across the escarpment and descends toward the coast. Descending air is compressed by the denser air beneath it and warms at the dry adiabatic lapse rate of about 1 degree Celsius per 100 metres. Over a descent of 1 800 metres the warming is 1 800 divided by 100 multiplied by 1 degree, which is 18 degrees Celsius, so the air arrives at 12 plus 18, that is 30 degrees Celsius. Because the air gains heat without gaining any moisture, its capacity to hold water rises sharply while its water content stays the same, so relative humidity collapses and the air becomes exceptionally dry. Hot, dry, gusty air over cured vegetation is the classic fire-weather combination, which is why berg winds bring extreme fire danger to the Cape and east coasts, and they typically arrive about a day ahead of an approaching cold front.
